newsitem.title: CANADA: Saudi in Canada wanted on bombing could be deported.
newsitem.headline: Saudi in Canada wanted on bombing could be deported.

text.p: Canada might deport a Saudi man whom the FBI wants to question about a bombing in Saudi Arabia that killed 19 U.S. troops, if hearings in Ottawa determined this would be merited, immigration officials said on Monday.

The man, Hani Abdel-Rahim Hussein al-Sayegh, was arrested in Ottawa last Tuesday on the grounds that he represented "a security risk to Canada," said Benoit Chiquette, spokesman for Immigration Minister Lucienne Robillard.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation said on Saturday that it hoped to be able to question Sayegh about the deadly truck bomb attack on an apartment complex housing U.S. troops in Dhahran last June.

In Washington, a U.S. law enforcement official said that based on interviews conducted by Saudi Arabia of other alleged participants in the attack, Sayegh was suspected of being the driver of a get-away car used after the bombing.
"We think he's an inner-circle person, a support person. He wasn't a bit player," the official said. "He's a good suspect."

The process will have to pass a number of legal tests, but Robillard has indicated a willingness to deport -- or "remove" -- people who are security risks even if there was a possibility that they could face the death penalty abroad.

"The minister was asked that question on Friday, and her answer was very clear, that obviously we always look at the personal risk related to removing an individual, but the most important issue at stake in making decisions about removal is always the safety and security of Canadians," Chiquette said.
Sayegh is being detained at an Ottawa prison where another Saudi, Fahad al-Shehri, is also being held.

Canadian officials say Shehri was arrested in December after he sought to become a refugee, supposedly because he said the Saudi government wanted him in connection with the June bombing of military housing in eastern Saudi Arabia.
He denies involvement in the bombing, however, and the Saudi government also denies wanting him. U.S. officials also denied having any interest in Shehri.
Sayegh, in contrast, would be valuable if the reports about him are confirmed.
The unusual FBI statement said it was grateful for Canada's vigilant actions that it hoped would "assist the United States and Saudi Arabia in the ongoing investigation of the Khobar Towers bombing."
It said the Saudi government provided "equally invaluable assistance leading to the identification and location of Al-Sayegh."

A Canadian Federal Court judge must review Sayegh's case this week to determine whether there had been grounds to issue the security certificate -- signed by Robillard and Solicitor-General Herb Gray -- that led to his arrest.
A date for the closed-door session has not been released but it was required to be held by Thursday or Friday, officials said.
If the process was determined to be valid, Sayegh would then appear at an immigration hearing to determine whether he should be deported, Chiquette said.
Neither he nor Gray's spokesman Dan Brien were aware of any formal request from the United States or Saudi Arabia for Sayegh's extradition.

The Washington Post quoted U.S. officials as saying they believed Sayegh was Shi'ite -- from the more radical branch of Islam practiced in Iran and by a minority of Saudis, mainly in the east of the country. It said Saudi officials suspect Shi'ite members of Saudi Hezbollah carried out the bombing.
The newspaper quoted a Saudi dissident as saying the Sayegh family was from the eastern village of Tarut, 25 miles (40 km) northwest of the site of the bombing.
